I Can't Even
eye KANT EE-vun
phrase (Millennial slang)
A truncated sentence ("I can’t even [deal with this / begin to express this]") used to signal emotion so overwhelming that words fail. It spread on Tumblr around 2011–2012 and became a Millennial catchphrase by 2013, often intensified as "I literally can’t even," "I can’t even right now," or simply "I can’t." It was used for joy (a cute puppy), outrage, and embarrassment alike, and was widely parodied as emblematic of Millennial speech.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

I can’t even is the sentence that gives up halfway: the speaker is so overwhelmed, by delight, exasperation, or disbelief, that she cannot finish. It is usually comic, a performance of being speechless. The Christian observation: speechlessness has a real place in Scripture, and it is worth teaching what it is for. Some things are too great or too terrible for words. When Job’s friends saw his suffering, "they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great" (Job 2:13); that was their wisest moment. The Psalmist confesses, "I am so troubled that I cannot speak" (Psa 77:4). And the Holy Spirit Himself prays for believers who run out of words: "the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered" (Rom 8:26). The difference between that silence and the Millennial "I can’t even" is direction and proportion. The biblical silence is poured out before God ("pour out your heart before him," Psa 62:8); the catchphrase performs emotion for an audience, often about something small. Proverbs warns that "A fool uttereth all his mind" (Pro 29:11), and the constant display of overwhelm can become a kind of emotional self-indulgence. A father teaches his children to feel deeply, to be honest when words fail, and to take that wordless feeling to the Lord, who understands groans.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial catchphrase (Tumblr, 2011–2013) for emotion too great for words; Scripture honours true speechlessness poured out before God (Rom 8:26; Psa 62:8) and cautions against performed overwhelm (Pro 29:11).

I CAN’T EVEN, phr. (Millennial slang, c. 2011–present) Expresses being overwhelmed beyond words, comically or sincerely. Variants: "I literally can’t even," "I can’t."

Decode for parents: notice whether your child’s overwhelm is a joke, a performance, or a cry; the last kind needs you.

Key Scripture

Job 2:13 — "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great."

Psa 77:4 — "Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak."

Rom 8:26 — "Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered."

Psa 62:8 — "Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah."

Pro 29:11 — "A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards."

Modern Corruption

I can’t even performs overwhelm for an audience, often over trifles; Scripture honours true wordlessness and directs it to God, who hears groanings that cannot be uttered.

expand to see more

The corruption is emotional inflation and display. The catchphrase makes being overwhelmed a constant public state, so that small things get the language of collapse and real collapse has no language left. It can also excuse a refusal to think: "I can’t even" ends a conversation that needed finishing. A generation trained to perform its feelings may find it hard to govern them.

The redemption is the honest silence turned toward God. The Psalms are full of men who could not finish their sentences and finished them in prayer; the Spirit carries what we cannot say. Teach the young to keep strong words for strong things, to sit silently with the grieving as Job’s friends did on their best days, and when they truly cannot even, to say so to their Father, who knows what they need before they ask.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English efne (even, level, "just") → intensifying even → truncated "I can’t even" (Tumblr, c. 2011) → 2013 catchphrase.
